Demander l’asile quelques semaines avant: Claiming asylum a few weeks before giving birth: Désirée’s administrative nightmare
Désirée était promise à un avenir au Roy: Désirée had a future ahead of her in the United Kingdom. Now she is an asylum seeker who doesn’t speak French and fears giving birth without her husband.
<strong><em>*Attention, cet article décr: *Warning: this article describes scenes of violence.
Désirée* est entrée en février 2023 comm: Désirée* entered Canada as a tourist in February 2023 to give a conference talk in Vancouver. Her plan was to have her research published after the conference so she could be admitted to a doctoral program in England, where she had been living for almost a year. For the one-week trip, she packed a small suitcase with a few clothes, and brought along a small “surprise” passenger. A few weeks before leaving, she had learned she was pregnant. Her husband encouraged her to make the short trip to Canada because, as usual, he supported her in her plans. They would not see each other again, or at least not for quite some time.
Pour comprendre comment une jeune diplôm: To understand how a brilliant young graduate holding a UK work visa ends up claiming asylum in Canada and living in a Montréal shelter, without speaking French, anxious about giving birth far from her husband and loved ones, and fearing she will have to keep running to stay alive, you have to know her long and painful journey.
<strong>Vivre dans les bidonvilles de Bu: Living in the slums of Bukavu, at the mercy of armed groups
Désirée est née dans les bidonvilles de: Désirée was born in the slums of Bukavu, a city in South Kivu, in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, on the border with Rwanda. <l1>In this region, coveted for its resources, militia attacks are a regular occurrence. </l1>One morning, men burst into her home. Désirée, then 20, and her 12-year-old nephew were abducted before their parents’ eyes.

The horror was only beginning. Three men raped her. “I don’t know if I’ll ever heal from this trauma. The only way to keep going with my life, at the time, was to stop thinking about it. But it still affects me.” While raping her, one of the men tortured her by driving needles all over her body. She would be left with a panic-level fear of needles, and therefore of the medical world, which would complicate her prenatal care at the hospital.
‍\nÀ la faveur d’une fusillade, elle s’é:
‍
During a shootout, she escaped with her nephew after several days in captivity. Together, they crossed the border into Rwanda and met a man who would change their lives. He was a truck driver, and he hid them aboard his truck to help them flee. “This man saved us by hiding us in the structure of the truck, under the cargo. He stopped whenever he could to give us water and food, and so we could relieve ourselves in the forest. I think we spent four or five days in his truck. He came from North Africa and had a Muslim name, that’s all I know about him. I don’t know what became of him, but I still pray for him,” Désirée recalls, emotional.
‍\n<strong>Du statut de réfugiée à la ma: ‍ From refugee status to a master’s degree in health innovation
‍\nC’est donc cachés dans ce camion qu’i:
‍
Hidden in that truck, they reached South Africa… 4,000 km from home. Alone, with no money or food, speaking neither English nor Swahili, they were taken in by a church. The pastor’s wife accompanied Désirée to the hospital, where she finally saw a doctor for the first time, several weeks after being raped. “That’s when I realized what had happened to me. During my flight, I was in survival mode. There, I could finally begin to heal. I started therapy that lasted five years. It allowed me to give value back to my life.”
Her refugee status, granted after a year of waiting, allowed her to receive a scholarship to begin higher education in English and information technology. She felt her life starting over: “That scholarship gave me back my smile and my hope.” Unfortunately, her nephew would not share that hope for better days; he fell into delinquency. “My nephew was angry and traumatized; I didn’t have the tools to help him, since I was in post-traumatic shock myself. He let himself be persuaded by violence, and we lost touch.”
‍\nElle poursuit ses études en Afrique d:
‍
She continued her studies in South Africa up to a master’s degree in health innovation, and got married. Little by little, she regained her balance thanks to therapy and managed to get in touch with her parents, from whom she had had no news since her abduction. A month later, her mother died. She never had the chance to see her again. She did experience the joy of being reunited with her father, whom she managed to bring to South Africa as a refugee. But misfortune kept striking, and he too died some time after arriving. “I was so happy to see him again. One day, I invited him to eat a Congolese dish. After the meal, we walked on the beach. That’s where he was struck by paralysis. He died a week later. The reunion was short, but it was a wonderful time for both of us. His death caused me great pain.”
‍\nSi Désirée mène une existence relativ:
‍
Although Désirée led a relatively stable life in South Africa, she was still the victim of xenophobic acts. These are numerous in a country that took in 266,700 refugees and asylum seekers in 2020, according to the UN Refugee Agency. Faced with a surge in attacks against refugee communities, she was forced to move yet again to escape the violence.
Fuir de nouveau la violence, de l’Anglet: Fleeing violence once more, from England to Quebec
‍\nC’est alors qu’une occasion professio:
‍
Then a professional opportunity came her way. She was recruited for a job in the United Kingdom. The recruiter, who had travelled to South Africa, promised her the moon — a work visa, company housing, a good salary — but there was a catch: she had to pay him to be hired. The prospect of a better life was tempting. Désirée paid the man and obtained a visa for herself and her husband. Of course, the British company was unaware of its employee’s misconduct. When Désirée arrived in England, she reported the crooked recruiter. That provoked the man’s fury, and he turned out to be a dangerous predator. Desperate because he had lost his livelihood and, above all, his position of power, he never stopped stalking her, harassing her and threatening her with death. No matter how many times she changed her phone number and her job, she knew her life was in danger. The man would not stop.
‍\nPour lui échapper, elle fuit et s’ins:
‍
To escape him, she fled and settled with her husband in another city, several hundred kilometres away. The fresh start was a chance for her to go back to school. She applied to a doctoral program, and her university advised her to get an article published to improve her chances of admission. That is how she came to be in Vancouver. The conference went well, until she received a call: the recruiter had found her again and intended to carry out his threat to kill her. He knew where she worked, and probably where she lived. She was pregnant, and her husband, who was away on a trip, would not be able to defend her if she returned. She could not face him. She knew she could call the police and confront him, but she is also a survivor of rape and of war, and she suffers from post-traumatic stress. Even though her whole life was in England, she refused to put her baby in danger. Fear won out. She decided not to go back and to claim asylum in Canada.
‍\nOn lui conseille d’aller à Montréal p:
‍
She was advised to go to Montréal to be closer to the Congolese community. There, the shock of the Quebec winter awaited her. She had packed clothes for only one week. When she arrived, she heard about a woman who had died of cold after spending a night on the street. Once again, she found herself alone, with nowhere to go. Her funds were dwindling. After a few weeks living in motels and looking for help to claim asylum, she tried to find a place in a shelter for refugees.
‍\n<strong>Un labyrinthe administratif p: ‍ An administrative maze for those without the “brown paper”
‍\nSa situation est compliquée : elle n’:
‍
Her situation was complicated: she didn’t have the “brown paper,” the official asylum seeker’s document issued by the government. Every organization told her the same thing: it is the key to everything — housing, food, social services… To receive official assistance, you have to have been identified by official organizations and appear in their records. Désirée did not enter Canada as an asylum seeker, but as a tourist.
‍\nUn long parcours se dessine devant el:
‍
A long road lay ahead of her, and her anxiety grew as she watched her belly get rounder day by day. She was temporarily housed in a women’s shelter. In addition to the “brown paper,” refugee aid organizations asked for references from social workers, which Désirée didn’t have, because she didn’t have the… “brown paper.” She moved from shelter to shelter. After numerous interviews, she was finally accepted into a shelter for refugees. She needed prenatal care, but here again, that famous paper was required. The office of the NGO Médecins du Monde was the only place where she could see a doctor. She had her first medical visit since arriving in Canada. For the first time, she heard her baby’s heartbeat. She thought of her husband, who would have so loved to be present at the birth, but who had not been granted a tourist visa to enter the country.
‍\nSans « papier brun », elle ne peut pa:
‍
Without the “brown paper,” she also could not give birth in a hospital. Médecins du Monde therefore referred her to a birth centre where midwives accept patients regardless of their status, after reviewing their history. It was a relief for her to finally receive care, especially from women, in a setting with little medical intervention, given her trauma.
<strong>‍</strong>\n<strong>Vivre sa gro: ‍ Going through pregnancy in fear of losing her housing
‍\nLe centre d’hébergement lui fournit d:
‍
The shelter provides her with food and transit passes, and helped her find an immigration lawyer. Once her asylum claim was submitted, she received a “white paper,” meaning the acknowledgement of receipt of her claim, which gives her partial medical coverage and a small allowance. “At that point, I tell myself that I have a roof over my head, an allowance, a midwife. For now, it’s okay,” Désirée explains. What she essentially lacks is a work permit, which is granted once the brown paper is received. So she is waiting for the judge’s decision. In reality, it is still possible that the judge will deny her refugee status. Her lawyer explained to her that a person can only be a refugee in one country, because all asylum claims are centralized by the UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency. And she has already been granted asylum in South Africa. So it will be difficult.
‍
The difficulties don’t end there. When she gives birth, Désirée will no longer be able to stay in her shelter, which is reserved for single women. She will have to find an apartment… but without a salary, that will be a nearly impossible mission. Adding up her allowance and the allowance for the baby, she will receive $870 a month. It is impossible to find an apartment in Montréal on that income. She will also have to find a daycare. The difficulty of getting a spot is well known, especially since many daycares only accept infants from a certain age. Without maternity leave, Désirée will have to work as soon as possible. If she finally gets her work permit, she hopes to find a job related to her master’s degree. But here again, she would need Quebec experience to hope to be hired.
‍\n« À chaque contraction, j’angoisse et:
‍
“With every contraction, I panic and I pray that I won’t give birth too quickly, because that would mean I no longer have a place to live. The only positive thing is that my child will be Canadian. I didn’t even know that when I got here!”
Still, Désirée hasn’t lost her smile or her hope. The war survivor has proven her resilience. But she finds herself trapped in a system she does not trust: at every danger, she fled, fearing men and authorities. If she cannot find refuge in Canada for herself and her baby, she will keep on fleeing.
